# Worksheet: what the data would have looked like

**~45 minutes**

The [chapter](../../chapters/07-observation-models.qmd) separated the *process*,
the epidemic itself, from the *observation*, the counts a surveillance system
produces. Here you run the same baseline epidemic through three increasingly
uncomfortable surveillance systems: one that misses most cases, one whose counts
are far noisier than a Poisson model allows, and one that reports differently on
different days of the week.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Parts A and B are the session.** **Part C** goes further if you get there; not
reaching it is completely fine. Worked solutions are posted at the end of each
day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

**New to Julia?** The
[Julia essentials worksheet](../prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd)
opens with an R-to-Julia table. `rand.(rng, Poisson.(v))` is the dotted call
from that table twice over: one draw per element of `v`.

::: {.callout-note}
Everything here *simulates* data from known parameters. Going the other way,
recovering the parameters from data, is parameter estimation and Bayesian
inference, which this workshop points to rather than teaches. The two chapters
are in the book for self-study, and the closing session names an external course
that covers them properly.
:::

## Setup

The process model is the baseline SIR with a fourth state $C$ that accumulates
infections, so that daily incidence is the increment of $C$.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch07-setup
using CairoMakie
using Distributions
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

function sir_cumulative!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R, C = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I
    du[3] = p.γ * I
    du[4] = λ * S            # C only ever increases
    return nothing
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0]
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
obsdays = 1:40

solution = solve(ODEProblem(sir_cumulative!, u0, (0.0, 40.0), p), Tsit5();
                 saveat = 1.0, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
cumulative = Array(solution)[4, :]
incidence = cumulative[2:end] .- cumulative[1:(end - 1)]   # latent xₜ

println("latent cases over 40 days: ", round(sum(incidence); digits = 1))
println("latent peak: day ", argmax(incidence), ", ",
        round(maximum(incidence); digits = 1), " new cases")
```

---

## Part A — only some cases are reported (~15 min)

The chapter reported every case, $\rho = 1$, to isolate the observation noise.
Real surveillance sees a fraction. With a reporting fraction $\rho$, the expected
count on day $t$ is $\rho x_t$, and the report is a Poisson draw around it:

$$
Y_t \mid x_t \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\rho\, x_t).
$$

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch07-a1
ρ = 0.4                       # two cases in five reach the surveillance system

expected = incidence          # TODO: the expected count is not the latent count
reported = zeros(Int, length(expected))   # TODO: one Poisson draw per day,
                                          # using rand.(StableRNG(20250801), ...)

check("expected counts are a fraction of the latent ones",
      isapprox(sum(expected), ρ * sum(incidence); rtol = 1e-8))
check("the reports are random, not the expected values",
      any(reported .!= round.(Int, expected)))
check("about ρ of the cases were reported",
      abs(sum(reported) / sum(incidence) - ρ) < 0.06)
check("the reported peak is within two days of the latent peak",
      abs(argmax(reported) - argmax(incidence)) <= 2)

(; latent_total = round(sum(incidence); digits = 1),
   reported_total = sum(reported),
   latent_peak_day = argmax(incidence),
   reported_peak_day = argmax(reported))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A

```julia
expected = ρ .* incidence
reported = rand.(StableRNG(20250801), Poisson.(expected))
```

`Poisson.(expected)` builds one distribution per day, and `rand.` draws one
number from each. Both dots are doing the same job as `sapply` would in R.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch07-reporting
#| fig-cap: "Latent daily incidence and the reported counts under 40% reporting."
fig = Figure(size = (760, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "new cases per day")
barplot!(ax, collect(obsdays), reported; color = (:steelblue, 0.6),
         label = "reported")
lines!(ax, collect(obsdays), incidence; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "latent incidence")
lines!(ax, collect(obsdays), expected; color = :black, linestyle = :dash,
       linewidth = 2, label = "ρ × latent")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### A1. Match the peak, not the epidemic

The dashed expectation is exactly the latent curve multiplied by $\rho$, so it
keeps the latent curve's shape and timing. Could a smaller epidemic produce the
same peak height under full reporting? The code below searches over
$\beta$ while keeping $N$, the initial state, $c$ and $\gamma$ fixed.

It matches the peak of the **expected** reported curve, not the random maximum of
`reported`: a noisy maximum would make the comparison depend on one lucky draw.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch07-a2
function incidence_at_beta(β)
    pβ = merge(p, (β = β,))
    solβ = solve(ODEProblem(sir_cumulative!, u0, (0.0, 40.0), pβ), Tsit5();
                 saveat = 1.0, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
    Cβ = Array(solβ)[4, :]
    return Cβ[2:end] .- Cβ[1:(end - 1)]
end

target_peak = maximum(expected)
β_candidates = range(0.025, 0.050; length = 251)
candidate_curves = incidence_at_beta.(β_candidates)
peak_errors = abs.([maximum(curve) for curve in candidate_curves] .- target_peak)

best = 1                       # TODO: index of the smallest value in peak_errors
β_match = β_candidates[best]
matched = candidate_curves[best]

check("the full-reporting curve matches the expected reported peak",
      abs(maximum(matched) - target_peak) < 0.2)

(; β_match = round(β_match; digits = 4),
   expected_peak = round(target_peak; digits = 1),
   expected_peak_day = argmax(expected),
   matched_peak_day = argmax(matched),
   expected_total = round(sum(expected); digits = 1),
   matched_total = round(sum(matched); digits = 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — matching the peak

`argmin` returns the index of the smallest value:

```julia
best = argmin(peak_errors)
```

The matching value is therefore `β_candidates[best]`, and the corresponding
incidence curve is `candidate_curves[best]`.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch07-matched-peak
#| fig-cap: "Two expected series with the same peak height: 40% reporting at the baseline transmission probability, and full reporting at a lower transmission probability."
fig = Figure(size = (760, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "expected cases per day")
lines!(ax, collect(obsdays), expected; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "ρ = 0.4, β = 0.05")
lines!(ax, collect(obsdays), matched; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3,
       linestyle = :dash, label = "ρ = 1, β = $(round(β_match; digits = 4))")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### A2. Interpret

- Why does the expected reported curve look like a smaller epidemic even though
  only the observation process changed? Distinguish the smooth expectation from
  the noisy `reported` bars.
- The second figure gives two expected series with nearly identical peak heights.
  Compare their early growth, peak day, width and 40-day cumulative total. Which
  features still reveal that they came from different $\beta$ values?
- When could you rely on those differences to distinguish $\rho$ from $\beta$?
  Consider what must be known about $N$, the initial state, $c$, $\gamma$ and the
  reporting process, and what a short or noisy series would change.

## Part B — counts noisier than Poisson (~15 min)

A Poisson model forces the variance to equal the mean. Surveillance counts are
often **overdispersed**: reports may arrive in batches, clusters may be tested
together, or one care home may contribute twenty cases on one day. The negative
binomial is a convenient marginal model for that extra variation: it keeps the
same mean and adds a dispersion parameter $r$, with

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_t] = \rho x_t + \frac{(\rho x_t)^2}{r},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{Var}[Y_t]}{\mathbb{E}[Y_t]} = 1 + \frac{\rho x_t}{r}.
$$

Small $r$ means very noisy; as $r$ grows the Poisson model comes back. Here you
measure that ratio by brute force on the peak day.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch07-b1
# NegativeBinomial(r, q) with mean μ needs q = r / (r + μ).
nb(μ, r) = NegativeBinomial(r, r / (r + μ))

peak_day = argmax(expected)
μ_peak = expected[peak_day]

# TODO: fill this list with three values of r, one of which you work out rather
# than guess. Using Var/E = 1 + μ/r from above, which r makes the variance on the
# peak day exactly twice the mean? Add one well below it and one well above.
dispersions = Float64[]

for r in dispersions
    rng = StableRNG(11)
    draws = [rand(rng, nb(μ_peak, r)) for _ in 1:2000]
    println("r = ", r,
            " | variance/mean = ", round(var(draws) / mean(draws); digits = 2),
            " | predicted 1 + μ/r = ", round(1 + μ_peak / r; digits = 2))
end

ratio(r) = (rng = StableRNG(11);
            draws = [rand(rng, nb(μ_peak, r)) for _ in 1:2000];
            var(draws) / mean(draws))

check("three dispersions tried", length(dispersions) == 3)
if length(dispersions) == 3
    ratios = ratio.(dispersions)
    check("larger r gives counts closer to Poisson",
          ratios[argmax(dispersions)] < ratios[argmin(dispersions)])
    check("the measured ratio matches the formula",
          all(abs.(ratios .- (1 .+ μ_peak ./ dispersions)) ./
              (1 .+ μ_peak ./ dispersions) .< 0.2))
    check("one of your three doubles the variance on the peak day",
          any(abs.(ratios .- 2) .< 0.3))
end
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B

Setting the ratio to 2 gives

$$
1 + \frac{\mu_{\text{peak}}}{r} = 2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
r = \mu_{\text{peak}},
$$

so the dispersion that doubles the variance is just the mean count on that day.
Print `μ_peak` and use it. Then bracket it, for example

```julia
dispersions = [1.0, round(μ_peak), 50.0]
```

Write them as `1.0` rather than `1`: `nb` divides by `r + μ`, and keeping
everything floating-point avoids surprises.

Note what this says: "overdispersed" is not a property of $r$ alone. The same
$r$ is close to Poisson on a day with two cases and wildly overdispersed at the
peak, because the ratio depends on $\mu/r$.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch07-dispersion
#| fig-cap: "One realisation of reported cases under a strongly overdispersed model (r = 1) and a closer-to-Poisson one (r = 50)."
# One stream per series, advanced across days. Rebuilding the RNG inside the
# comprehension would restart it and reuse the same draw every day.
noisy_rng, tidy_rng = StableRNG(31), StableRNG(32)
noisy  = [rand(noisy_rng, nb(μ, 1.0)) for μ in expected]
tidy   = [rand(tidy_rng, nb(μ, 50.0)) for μ in expected]

fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
for (k, (series, title)) in enumerate(zip((noisy, tidy),
                                          ("r = 1 (overdispersed)", "r = 50")))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, k]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "reported cases",
              title = title)
    barplot!(ax, collect(obsdays), series; color = (:steelblue, 0.6))
    lines!(ax, collect(obsdays), expected; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3)
    ylims!(ax, 0, 60)
end
fig
```

### B1. Interpret

- On the peak day the expected count is about 18. Read off the variance-to-mean
  ratio at $r = 1$ and say, in cases, roughly how far a single day's report can
  sit from its expectation.
- Both panels of the figure come from the same epidemic and the same reporting
  fraction. If you were handed only the left panel, what would you be tempted to
  conclude about the epidemic that would be wrong?

## Part C — the weekend effect (optional)

*Start this only if you have finished Part B.*

Both models so far assume every day is observed the same way. Real notification
data often has a strong weekly rhythm, with fewer reports at the weekend and more
on weekdays. Nothing about the epidemic changes, only the reporting.

Below, a weight is applied to each day of the week before the Poisson draw. Fill
in weights that report more than average on the five weekdays and much less at
the weekend, and that average to one across the week.

Averaging to one keeps the overall total roughly unchanged, but only roughly.
Exact cancellation would need the weights to be uncorrelated with incidence, and
they are not: while the epidemic is growing, the later days of each week carry
more cases than the earlier ones, so a low weekend weight removes more than its
share. Keep an eye on how close the two totals come.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch07-c1
# One weight per day of the week, Monday first. Day 1 of the epidemic is a Monday.
weekday_weights = fill(1.0, 7)     # TODO: replace with a weekday/weekend pattern

weight(t) = weekday_weights[mod1(t, 7)]
is_weekend(t) = mod1(t, 7) in (6, 7)

# Each day draws from the same seed in both series, which couples them: the two
# see matched randomness, so the comparison is less noisy than two independent
# runs would be. It does not make either series noise-free.
patterned = [rand(StableRNG(4000 + t), Poisson(ρ * incidence[t] * weight(t)))
             for t in obsdays]
uniform   = [rand(StableRNG(4000 + t), Poisson(ρ * incidence[t]))
             for t in obsdays]

# Pearson dispersion: mean squared deviation from the expected count, in units
# of that count. A correct Poisson model gives about 1.
dispersion(series) =
    mean(((series[t] - ρ * incidence[t])^2) / (ρ * incidence[t]) for t in obsdays)

observed_ratio = [patterned[t] / (ρ * incidence[t]) for t in obsdays]

check("the weights average to one and vary across the week",
      isapprox(mean(weekday_weights), 1.0; atol = 0.02) &&
      std(weekday_weights) > 0.1)
check("weekends report less than weekdays",
      mean(observed_ratio[is_weekend.(obsdays)]) <
      mean(observed_ratio[.!is_weekend.(obsdays)]) - 0.3)
check("the totals are still comparable",
      abs(sum(patterned) - sum(uniform)) / sum(uniform) < 0.15)
check("ignoring the pattern looks like overdispersion",
      dispersion(patterned) > 2 * dispersion(uniform))

(; total_patterned = sum(patterned), total_uniform = sum(uniform),
   dispersion_patterned = round(dispersion(patterned); digits = 2),
   dispersion_uniform = round(dispersion(uniform); digits = 2))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C

```julia
weekday_weights = [1.3, 1.3, 1.3, 1.3, 1.3, 0.3, 0.2]
```

Five weekdays at 1.3 and a weekend at 0.3 and 0.2 average to exactly 1.0.
`mod1(t, 7)` is the day of the week: it is like `t % 7` but returns 7 rather
than 0, so it indexes the vector directly.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch07-weekend
#| fig-cap: "Reported cases with a day-of-week reporting pattern. The expected count under a model that ignores the pattern is drawn through it."
fig = Figure(size = (760, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "reported cases")
barplot!(ax, collect(obsdays), patterned;
         color = [is_weekend(t) ? (:grey, 0.8) : (:steelblue, 0.6) for t in obsdays])
lines!(ax, collect(obsdays), ρ .* incidence; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "ρ × latent")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### C1. Interpret

- The last check says that a Poisson model which ignores the weekly pattern sees
  the data as overdispersed. Explain why, and say what that does to a reported
  uncertainty interval around $\beta$. How sure can you be about the *direction*
  of that change?
- Name two ways to handle this. Which of them changes the observation model and
  which changes the data?
